stem: During an outage of the central authentication service, a badge-controlled server room falls back to denying all entry until service is restored. Which secure design principle does this illustrate?
explanations: Failing securely means a component defaults to a secure, denying state when an error or outage occurs — exactly what the fallback behavior shows.
Least privilege limits the rights granted during normal operation; it says nothing about how a component behaves when it fails.
Separation of duties splits sensitive tasks between people to deter fraud; it does not describe failure behavior of a control.
Defense in depth layers multiple controls so one failure is not fatal; the scenario describes a single control's failure state, not layering.

stem: A vendor distributes firmware updates through public mirrors and must let devices confirm that each image is authentic and unmodified before installation. Which mechanism BEST meets this requirement?
options: A digital signature over each firmware image
A SHA-256 hash published beside each image
An HMAC computed with a shared device key
TLS encryption for every download session
explanations: A signature made with the vendor's private key gives both integrity and origin authenticity, and every device can verify it with an embedded public key without sharing any secret.
A hash alone proves integrity but not origin: an attacker who replaces the image on a mirror can just as easily replace the published hash beside it.
An HMAC requires the same secret in every device; extracting the key from any one device lets an attacker forge updates for all of them.
TLS protects data only in transit; a compromised mirror serves a tampered image over a perfectly valid TLS session.
